artworks.description:
This painting beautifully portrays Lord Krishna in his youthful form, radiating divine charm, innocence, and serenity. Every element of the artwork has been thoughtfully composed to reflect his connection with nature, beauty, devotion, and music.

At the top, Krishna is adorned with an elaborate mukut (crown), richly decorated with golden ornaments and red gemstone details. The crown is surrounded by vibrant peacock feathers, one of the most iconic symbols associated with Krishna, representing beauty, grace, and divine playfulness. Nestled within the mukut are blooming pink lotuses, adding a sense of purity, love, and spiritual beauty.

His dark, flowing hair frames his gentle face, while a soft decorative cloth wraps gracefully around his head. His expressive eyes, delicately shaped eyebrows, and calm gaze capture the youthful innocence and enchanting charm of Krishna. The subtle smile on his lips adds warmth and a sense of divine peace.

He wears elegant golden earrings adorned with red stones, complementing the richness of his crown. A radiant yellow garment, reminiscent of Krishna's traditional Pitambar, forms a vibrant backdrop around him and brings warmth to the composition.

In his hands rests the golden bansuri (flute), decorated with delicate floral details. The flute symbolizes Krishna's divine music—believed to captivate not only people but all of nature. The flowers surrounding it further enhance the connection between Krishna, music, and the natural world.

Finally, adorning his neck is a beautiful floral mala (garland) made of soft yellow blossoms. The mala adds a touch of devotion and purity, completing his divine appearance.

Together, the mukut, peacock feathers, lotuses, jewellery, flute, Pitambar, and floral mala create a harmonious portrayal of young Krishna—playful yet serene, youthful yet divine, and forever surrounded by the beauty of nature and devotion.
artworks.title: KRISHNA IN YOUTH AGE

artworks.description: M.A.R. Chughtai’s *Radhika* is a delicate watercolor that embodies both lyrical beauty and spiritual symbolism. The painting portrays Radhika with half‑closed eyes, her posture radiating tenderness and quiet longing. Draped in a soft violet *ghaghra* and a golden *chunri*, adorned with pearls and bangles, she becomes the epitome of grace and devotion. Chughtai’s fluid calligraphic lines elongate her figure, while the wash technique creates a glowing, dreamlike atmosphere. In her hand rests a lotus, symbolizing purity and divine love, while a hovering bee subtly alludes to Krishna’s presence. The lamp (*deeya*) beside her adds warmth and spiritual illumination, reinforcing the theme of inner light and hope. Every element—her attire, jewelry, expression, and the surrounding motifs—works in harmony to evoke the timeless essence of love, purity, and devotion.
artworks.title: Radhika by Mar Chughtai

artworks.description: a vibrant celebration of feminine grace and cultural heritage. The figures, dressed in richly colored saris of yellow, purple, and green, are adorned with jewelry that highlights refinement and prosperity. Each woman holds a pink lotus, a symbol of purity, beauty, and spiritual awakening, while the lush green leaves surrounding them enhance the sense of natural harmony. The jharokha, a traditional arched window, frames the trio like living sculptures, situating them within the grandeur of Indian architecture and evoking timeless elegance. The central figure in yellow draws immediate attention, while the flanking figures balance the composition, creating symmetry and unity. Together, the triadic arrangement suggests collective strength and harmony, while the lotus motif reinforces themes of devotion and transcendence. This artwork becomes more than a portrait—it is a poetic meditation on womanhood, tradition, and spiritual purity, radiating both aesthetic richness and cultural depth.
artworks.title: Three Women In Jharokha

artworks.description: This painting of Shiv–Shakti (Ardhanarishvara) beautifully embodies the union of masculine and feminine energies in Hindu philosophy. The left half, representing Lord Shiva, is marked by blue skin, the crescent moon in his hair, and the serpent coiled around his neck—symbols of ascetic power, cosmic rhythm, and transcendence. The right half, representing Goddess Parvati, glows with pinkish tones, adorned with jewelry like earrings and a nose ring, signifying fertility, beauty, and nurturing grace. The seamless blending of the two halves conveys balance and harmony, reminding us that creation itself arises from the union of opposites. The background, with its soft pink and purple hues, enhances the divine aura and suggests spiritual transcendence. Together, the composition becomes a meditation on wholeness: Shiva as consciousness and Parvati as energy, inseparable yet distinct, forming the eternal cycle of existence.
artworks.title: Shiv-Shakti

poems.title: Between Two Brushstrokes
poems.excerpt: I spilled a drop of morning rose upon the virgin linen, and watched the silence turn into a song...
poems.fullText:
I spilled a drop of morning rose
upon the virgin linen,
and watched the silence turn into a song.

We are all fragments of unfinished canvases,
searching for the shade of terracotta
that feels like coming home.

Under the shade of ancient college trees,
we paint what words dare not confess,
and let the wet pigment hold our quiet breath.

poems.title: Verses in the Library Hall
poems.excerpt: Old leather bindings smell of rain and centuries of longing. I left a poem between pages forty and four...
poems.fullText:
Old leather bindings smell of rain
and centuries of longing.
I left a poem between pages forty and four,
hoping someone with paint-stained fingers
might find it when the monsoon arrives.

You do not simply read art;
you allow it to undress your guarded thoughts
and leave them luminous in the dark.

poems.title: The Anatomy of a Sunrise
poems.excerpt: Crimson first, then whisper-pink, then all the world is gold...
poems.fullText:
Crimson first, then whisper-pink,
then all the world is gold.

Every daybreak is a masterwork
no painter can ever own,
yet we spend our lives with wet palettes,
trying to capture just one heartbeat of its grace.
